core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Appendicitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes keeping the patient NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia, pre-operative antibiotics, and urgent surgical consultation for appendectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: acute abdominal pain starting around belly button and moving to the right lower side

Key HPI features: 24M presents with 18 hours of abdominal pain that began as a dull ache around his umbilicus and has since migrated to the right lower quadrant, becoming sharp and constant. Reports loss of appetite and mild nausea.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.8C, HR 92, BP 122/76. Abdominal exam reveals localized tenderness and voluntary guarding at McBurney's point with a positive Rovsing's sign, no rebound or diffuse rigidity. Bloods: WBC 13,200 /uL with left shift. Abdominal CT with IV contrast shows a dilated, non-compressible appendix (9 mm) with periappendiceal fat stranding.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Appendicitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastroenteritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Diffuse rigidity or rebound tenderness — suggests perforation.
management_principles: Perform a focused abdominal exam (check McBurney point tenderness, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign)
Order CBC, CMP, and abdominal CT
Keep NPO, give IV fluids and analgesia, start pre-operative IV antibiotics, and refer urgently to general surgery for appendectomy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen causing pain that migrates from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant, with anorexia and low-grade fever.
red_flags: Diffuse rigidity or rebound tenderness — suggests perforation

must_ask.say: Did the pain start around your belly button and move to your lower right side?
Have you lost your appetite or felt nauseated?
Does moving or coughing make it worse?
Have you had pain like this before?

history.answer: My lower right belly has been hurting really badly since yesterday.
It started about 18 hours ago, yesterday afternoon, and it has been getting steadily worse.
At first it was a dull ache right around my belly button, but overnight it shifted down to the lower right side of my belly.
No, it does not radiate to my back, shoulder, or down toward my groin.
It started as a dull ache, but now it is a constant, sharp pain.
Right now it is around a 7 out of 10. It was about a 3 or 4 when it started around my belly button.
It hurts much more when I walk, cough, or move around. Lying completely still with my knees bent makes it a tiny bit better.
I have completely lost my appetite since yesterday and have not felt like eating anything.
I felt mildly nauseous starting last night, but I have not actually vomited.
I have not had a bowel movement today, but I do not have diarrhea and there is no blood. I was able to pass gas this morning.
I have been feeling somewhat warm and feverish today, but I have not had shaking chills.
No, my skin and eyes look normal, and my urine is not dark nor are my stools pale.
No burning or pain when I urinate, no blood in my urine, and I do not have to pee more often than usual.
No, I have not felt lightheaded, dizzy, or like I might faint.
No chest pain, shortness of breath, or cough.
history.topic: Chest pain or shortness of breath

history.answer: I just had a regular sandwich for lunch yesterday before this started; nothing greasy, spoiled, or unusual.
No, I have not taken any ibuprofen, aspirin, or other pain relievers.
No, I have never had an irregular heart rhythm, atrial fibrillation, or vascular disease.
No, I have never had abdominal pain like this before.
I wonder if it could be appendicitis or maybe severe food poisoning. I am really worried that my appendix might burst and that I will need emergency surgery.
I hope you can do a CT scan or ultrasound to find out what is wrong and give me something for the pain.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I drink occasionally with friends on weekends, but I have not had any alcohol in the past week.
I am a 24-year-old college student living in an apartment near campus.
No one in my family has serious gastrointestinal problems, though my cousin had his appendix removed a few years ago.
I am not currently sexually active and have no history of sexually transmitted infections.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, heart rate 92 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 37.8 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Lying still in bed appearing uncomfortable with hips slightly flexed, alert and oriented, no severe distress.
Flat, symmetric contour with no surgical scars, distension, caput medusae, or rashes.
Decreased, hypoactive bowel sounds throughout all four quadrants; no bruits heard.
Tympanic to percussion throughout; no shifting dullness or hepatosplenomegaly.
Soft abdomen with marked localized tenderness and voluntary guarding in the right lower quadrant; other quadrants non-tender.
No rebound tenderness and no involuntary muscular rigidity.
Positive McBurney point tenderness, positive Rovsing sign with right lower quadrant pain upon left lower quadrant palpation, and positive psoas sign.
Negative Murphy sign with no tenderness or inspiratory arrest during deep palpation of the right upper quadrant.
Normal sphincter tone, no palpable mass, no tenderness on rectal shelf, and no gross blood on examining glove.
